221.quote_or_event: “The effect of giving of the gift–dāna–has distinctions based on the specific manner in which it is given–vidhiviśeṣa, the specific thing given–dravyaviśeṣa, the specific nature of the giver–dātṛviśeṣa, and the specific nature of the recipient–pātraviśeṣa.” … “The presence of qualities which lead to salvation indicates the superiority of the recipient–pātraviśeṣa.”
221.explanation: Umāsvāti's sūtra, with Pūjyapāda's commentary, says that what a gift is worth depends partly on who receives it. For Pūjyapāda the best recipient is one whose qualities lead toward liberation.
221.tie_back: Valluvar also defines true giving by its recipient, though for him that recipient is the destitute person who cannot repay. Jain dāna theory ranks recipients by spiritual worth instead, so the two agree on the principle and differ on who should receive.
221.source: Tattvārtha Sūtra 7.39, with Pūjyapāda's Sarvārthasiddhi (tr. Vijay K. Jain, 2018; wisdomlib.org)
221._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on wisdomlib.org. Both texts make the recipient the measure of a gift, but the Jain criterion (fitness for liberation) is not the Kural's (destitution), and the idea of a gift as a disguised exchange is absent.

222.quote_or_event: “Is it, therefore, a reproach to a man if he starve and keep his integrity inviolate, rather than fill his stomach by the disgraceful practice of mendicity?”
222.explanation: In its chapter on the dread of begging, the Nālaṭiyār says it is better to go hungry with one's integrity intact than to live by asking others for food.
222.tie_back: This matches the first half of Valluvar's couplet: taking from others stays bad even when it is called a good path.
222.source: Nālaṭiyār, ch. 31 ('Dread of mendicity'), st. 2 (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)
222._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on wisdomlib.org; this Tamil Jain text covers only the 'receiving is bad' half, not 'giving is good even without heaven'. It also sits uneasily with Jain monastic practice, where monks live on alms by rule.

223.quote_or_event: “Not saying they have very little, not saying they have not anything, let them ever exercise fruitful charity to all. Like the pitcher of the mendicant who enters the house-door for alms, it will, in due course, gradually become full.”
223.explanation: The Nālaṭiyār tells people never to excuse themselves with 'I have little' or 'I have nothing', and to keep giving. Small gifts add up, it says, the way a mendicant's pitcher slowly fills.
223.tie_back: Valluvar finds nobility in giving without first uttering the miserable words 'I have nothing', and this stanza turns down exactly that excuse.
223.source: Nālaṭiyār, ch. 10 ('Liberality'), st. 9 (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)
223._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on wisdomlib.org; this is a Tamil Jain text and fits the giver-centred reading of the kural (Parimelazhagar), not the reading in which the asker says 'I have nothing'.

224.quote_or_event: “To those men the gates of heaven shall never be closed, who with tender hearts and with a mind in accordance with their alms, greatly rejoicing, give even in poverty according to their ability, even as they did in the day of prosperity.”
224.explanation: The Nālaṭiyār praises givers who give gladly, with tender hearts, and keep giving even when they have become poor.
224.tie_back: Valluvar describes the generous person's discomfort at being asked, which ends in joy once the asker is satisfied. The Nālaṭiyār likewise places the giver's joy and tender-heartedness at the centre of a true gift.
224.source: Nālaṭiyār, ch. 10 ('Liberality'), st. 1 (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)
224._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on wisdomlib.org; this is a Tamil Jain text. It shares the theme of the giver's joy but lacks the kural's turn from the pain of being asked to delight at the recipient's happy face.

225.quote_or_event: “By austerities he cuts off the Karman.” … “By doing service he acquires the Karman which brings about for him the nâman and gôtra of a Tîrthakara.”
225.explanation: In Mahāvīra's list of the fruits of religious practice, austerity (tapas) wears away karma. Service to others (vaiyāvṛttya) is said to earn the karma that makes one a future Tīrthaṅkara, the highest rank Jain tradition recognises.
225.tie_back: Valluvar ranks relieving others' hunger above the ascetic's power to endure hunger. This passage likewise gives service to others a spiritual fruit that austerity alone does not bring.
225.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 29.27 and 29.43 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
225._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on archive.sacred-texts.com. Jainism prizes fasting highly and does not explicitly rank service above it; the comparison is implied by the different fruits, and 'service' here means mainly service to monks rather than feeding the poor.

226.quote_or_event: “When by blameless means thou hast acquired great wealth, then eat with others rice imported by oxen, for wealth never remaineth in the centre with anyone, but changes its position like a cart-wheel.”
226.explanation: The Nālaṭiyār's chapter on unstable wealth says that wealth, once honestly gained, should be shared at the table, because riches never stay with anyone for long.
226.tie_back: Valluvar tells the person who has gained wealth to 'store' it in relieving others' hunger; the Nālaṭiyār gives the same advice for the same reason, that wealth kept to oneself does not last.
226.source: Nālaṭiyār, ch. 1 ('Unstable Wealth'), st. 2 (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)
226._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on wisdomlib.org; this is a Tamil Jain text. It shares the core advice to put acquired wealth into feeding others, but lacks the kural's image of hunger-relief as a treasury.

227.quote_or_event: “Give what you are able, even though you have not the thousandth part of a measure of rice in the house, and then eat your meal; the wise call those in this birth wandering beggars whose chimneys smoke not in this earth, surrounded by the deep sea, who gave not alms in a former birth.”
227.explanation: The Nālaṭiyār says to share some food before eating, however little one has. It explains present-day hunger and beggary as the karmic result of not giving in a former birth.
227.tie_back: Valluvar says hunger will hardly touch one who habitually shares food; the Nālaṭiyār makes the same link from the other side, since those who never shared become those whose cooking fires go out.
227.source: Nālaṭiyār, ch. 10 ('Liberality'), st. 4 (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)
227._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on wisdomlib.org; this is a Tamil Jain text. Its link between sharing and freedom from hunger is explicitly karmic across births, which the kural does not state.

228.quote_or_event: “They who, vexing their own bodies by stinting them in food and raiment, perform not acts of that goodly charity which never faileth, but avariciously hoard up what they have gathered together, will lose it all. O Lord of the mountain land which toucheth the sky! the bees which are driven from the honey they have collected bear witness.”
228.explanation: The Nālaṭiyār compares misers who neither give nor enjoy their wealth to bees driven from the honey they stored. Like the bees, such hoarders lose everything in the end.
228.tie_back: Valluvar mocks the hard-hearted who hoard only to lose it all, unaware of the joy of giving, and this stanza makes the same charge with the image of the robbed honeycomb.
228.source: Nālaṭiyār, ch. 1 ('Unstable Wealth'), st. 10 (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)
228._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on wisdomlib.org; this Tamil Jain text closely matches the hoard-and-lose theme, though it does not mention the kural's 'joy of giving'.

229.quote_or_event: “To give a part of their meal to the extent of their ability, both to the friendly and unfriendly, and after that to eat, is truly to eat a meal. To those who refuse their food to the needy, and so live and eat and pass on, the door of heaven will be closed.”
229.explanation: The Nālaṭiyār's chapter on illiberality says that only a meal shared first with others, whether friend or not, truly counts as eating. Those who eat without sharing have heaven closed to them.
229.tie_back: Valluvar calls solitary eating, done to keep one's stores full, more wretched than begging; the Nālaṭiyār likewise denies that unshared eating is a real meal at all.
229.source: Nālaṭiyār, ch. 28 ('Illiberality'), st. 1 (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)
229._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on wisdomlib.org; this is a Tamil Jain text. It condemns unshared eating as the kural does but lacks the deliberately shocking comparison with begging.

230.quote_or_event: Samantabhadra defines sallekhanā, the Jain practice of voluntarily giving up the body by gradual fasting, as something undertaken for the sake of dharma. It is permitted only when calamity, famine, old age or incurable disease makes it impossible to go on living righteously.
230.explanation: In Jain householder ethics, a person may calmly accept death when life can no longer be used to practise dharma. This 'wise death' is treated as a final religious act, not as a defeat.
230.tie_back: Valluvar says death becomes sweet when one can no longer give. Jainism also accepts death once a life can no longer serve its moral purpose, but for Jains that purpose is self-purification rather than giving.
230.source: Samantabhadra, Ratnakaraṇḍa Śrāvakācāra 122 (cf. tr. Champat Rai Jain, 1917)
230._accuracy_note: Paraphrase only: the verse's content was checked through a secondary (Wikipedia) rendering, not against Champat Rai Jain's translation. The parallel is structural, and sallekhanā has nothing to do with being unable to give.
